Based on my review of **SOP-LEGC-005** against the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR §§164.400–414) and De-identification Standard (§164.514), the following specific elements are **MISSING** from the SOP.

---

## I. HIPAA Breach Notification (§§164.400–414) — Missing Operational Procedures

| # | HIPAA Requirement | Citation | What the SOP Lacks |
|---|-------------------|----------|---------------------|
| 1 | **Dedicated HIPAA breach-notification procedure** — The SOP references a GDPR breach-notification template in ServiceNow (§5.2) but has **no equivalent template, workflow, or RACI for HIPAA breach notifications** to individuals, HHS, or media. | §164.404, §164.406, §164.408 | No HIPAA-specific notification template; no task type in Filing Calendar for HIPAA breach notifications. |
| 2 | **60-calendar-day deadline tracking** — “Without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery.” | §164.404(b), §164.406(b), §164.408(b)–(c) | KPI T-01 tracks general on-time filing rate but **no HIPAA-specific 60-day SLA or automated countdown** in ServiceNow. |
| 3 | **“Discovery” definition & trigger** — Breach deemed discovered when known or “by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known” to any workforce member/agent. | §164.404(a)(2) | No procedure to timestamp discovery, assess reasonable diligence, or log when the 60-day clock starts. |
| 4 | **Mandatory content elements for individual notices** — (A) description of breach, (B) types of PHI, (C) steps for individuals, (D) mitigation actions, (E) contact procedures (toll-free phone, email, website, or postal address). | §164.404(c)(1) | No content checklist or template ensuring these five elements are included in every HIPAA breach letter. |
| 5 | **Plain-language requirement** — Notification “shall be written in plain language.” | §164.404(c)(2) | No plain-language review gate (G2/G3) specific to breach notices. |
| 6 | **Media notification for breaches ≥500 residents of a State/jurisdiction** — Prominent media outlets, same 60-day deadline, same content. | §164.406 | No media-notification workflow, media-list maintenance, or approval gate for HIPAA media notices. |
| 7 | **HHS (Secretary) notification** — ≥500 individuals: contemporaneous via HHS portal; <500: annual log submitted within 60 days of calendar year-end. | §164.408(b)–(c) | No HHS portal submission procedure; no annual breach-log compilation process; no Filing Calendar entries for these obligations. |
| 8 | **Business Associate (BA) notification to Covered Entity** — BA must notify CE within 60 days of discovery, including identification of each affected individual. | §164.410 | SOP defines “BA” (§2) but **no BA breach-notification intake, tracking, or escalation procedure**. |
| 9 | **Substitute notice for insufficient/out-of-date contact info** — <10 individuals: alternative written/phone; ≥10: website posting (90 days) + toll-free phone (90 days). | §164.404(d)(2) | No substitute-notice procedure or template. |
| 10 | **Burden-of-proof documentation** — Covered entity/BA must demonstrate all notifications were made or that the incident was not a breach. | §164.414(b) | Archival (§5.5) is generic; **no breach-specific evidence package** (discovery log, notification copies, mailing logs, HHS portal receipts, media affidavits). |
| 11 | **Risk-assessment exception** — Breach notification not required if risk assessment demonstrates low probability of compromise (§164.402 definition of “breach”). | §164.402, §164.414(b) | No documented risk-assessment methodology, worksheet, or approval gate for “no-notification” determinations. |

---

## II. HIPAA De-identification (§164.514) — Missing Controls for Regulatory Filings

| # | HIPAA Requirement | Citation | What the SOP Lacks |
|---|-------------------|----------|---------------------|
| 12 | **De-identification method selection & documentation** — Either (1) Expert Determination (§164.514(b)(1)) with documented methods/results, or (2) Safe Harbor (§164.514(b)(2)) removing 18 identifiers. | §164.514(a)–(b) | **No procedure to de-identify PHI before inclusion in regulatory filings**; no expert-determination template; no Safe Harbor checklist. |
| 13 | **Limited Data Set (LDS) procedures** — LDS excludes direct identifiers but retains town/city/state/zip; requires Data Use Agreement (DUA) for research/public health/health care operations. | §164.514(e) | No LDS creation procedure; no DUA template or tracking for regulatory filings that use LDS. |
| 14 | **Re-identification controls** — Code must not be derived from PHI; must not be used/disclosed for other purposes; mechanism must not be disclosed. | §164.514(c) | No re-identification code management procedure for filings that use coded data. |
| 15 | **Minimum Necessary analysis for disclosures** — For routine disclosures: policies/procedures limiting PHI to amount reasonably necessary; for non-routine: criteria developed per request. | §164.514(d)(2)–(3) | Section 4.6 addresses GDPR personal data in filings but **no HIPAA minimum-necessary review gate** for PHI-containing submissions. |
| 16 | **Workforce access identification** — Identify persons/classes who need PHI access and the category/conditions of access. | §164.514(d)(2)(i)–(ii) | No PHI-access matrix for regulatory filing roles (RFO, Regulatory Operations Analyst, reviewers). |

---

## III. Structural Gaps in the SOP Framework

| Gap | Description |
|-----|-------------|
| **No HIPAA-specific Filing Calendar entries** | §5.1 annual scoping does not explicitly require populating HIPAA breach-notification obligations (individual, media, HHS, BA) with statutory citations, 60-day deadlines, and responsible owners. |
| **No HIPAA breach-notification RACI** | §3 assigns “Security Incident Response Lead” for “state breach notification laws and EU AI Act” but **omits HIPAA individual/HHS/media notification owners**. |
| **No HIPAA breach-notification review gates** | §5.3 G1–G5 gates are generic; **no gate validates 60-day timeline, content elements, plain language, or HHS portal submission**. |
| **No HIPAA breach-notification KPIs** | §7.1 tracks general on-time filing (T-01) but **no KPI for % of HIPAA breach notifications sent within 60 days, % with complete content, or % of HHS portal acknowledgments received**. |
| **No cross-reference to a HIPAA Breach Notification SOP** | §10 Related Policies lists GDPR (SOP-SECP-012), Model Risk (SOP-MRM-001), Records (SOP-DRM-003), but **no HIPAA breach notification or de-identification SOP is referenced**. |

---

## Summary of Missing Elements

| Category | Count | Critical Regulatory Citations |
|----------|-------|-------------------------------|
| Breach notification procedures | 11 | §§164.404, 164.406, 164.408, 164.410, 164.414 |
| De-identification / minimum necessary | 5 | §164.514(a)–(e) |
| SOP structural gaps | 5 | Framework omissions (Calendar, RACI, Gates, KPIs, References) |
| **Total** | **21** | |

---

## Recommendation
SOP-LEGC-005 functions as a **governance framework** but does not contain the **operational procedures** HIPAA requires for breach notification and de-identification. Meridian should either:
1. Create a companion **SOP-LEGC-005-HIPAA** (or SOP-SECP-XXX) dedicated to HIPAA breach notification and de-identification, referenced in §10; or
2. Expand SOP-LEGC-005 with HIPAA-specific appendices covering: (a) breach-notification workflow with 60-day countdown, content checklist, media/HHS/BA procedures, substitute notice, and burden-of-proof evidence package; (b) de-identification procedure (Expert Determination vs. Safe Harbor), LDS/DUA process, re-identification controls, and minimum-necessary review gate for filings.

**Compliance level: gap**

output.answer:
Based on my review of **SOP-AIML-006 (Model Performance Monitoring)** against **SR 11-7's ongoing monitoring expectations** (Sections V–VII), the following specific elements are **MISSING or INSUFFICIENT**:

---

### 1. **Formal Outcomes Analysis with Back-Testing & Outlier Analysis**
**SR 11-7 (Section V):** *"Outcomes analysis can take many forms, including testing conducted during model development, reports or analysis performed as part of ongoing monitoring, or standalone activities such as back-testing or outlier analysis."*

**SOP Gap:** The SOP monitors performance metrics against ground truth (Section 5.2) and runs daily ground-truth validation pipelines (Section 6.2), but it **does not define**:
- Periodic **back-testing** of model predictions against realized outcomes over extended horizons (e.g., quarterly/annual look-backs).
- Structured **outlier analysis** to identify systematic prediction failures in specific subpopulations or edge cases.
- A formal **outcomes analysis report** separate from incident-driven RCA.

---

### 2. **Periodic Reassessment of Model Limitations & Boundaries**
**SR 11-7 (Section V):** *"An effective ongoing monitoring plan may also include regularly assessing any model limitations at the development stage and over time..."*

**SOP Gap:** The SOP captures limitations at onboarding (Section 5.1) but **lacks a recurring process** to:
- Re-evaluate whether the model is being used **beyond its intended purpose/scope** (SR 11-7: *"Using a model beyond its intended purpose introduces additional uncertainty and risk"*).
- Update documented limitations as data distributions, products, or regulations evolve.
- Flag when production usage drifts from the original use case (e.g., clinical model applied to a new patient cohort).

---

### 3. **Aggregate / Portfolio-Level Model Risk Monitoring**
**SR 11-7 (Section III):** *"Sound practice involves assessing model risk both individually and in aggregate. Aggregate risk reflects interactions and dependencies among models; reliance on common assumptions, data, or methodologies..."*

**SOP Gap:** All monitoring is **per-model** (individual dashboards, per-model alerts, per-model KPIs). The SOP **does not**:
- Monitor correlated drift across models sharing features, training data, or upstream pipelines.
- Track concentration risk (e.g., multiple clinical models relying on the same EHR feed).
- Report aggregate model risk to governance bodies.

---

### 4. **Vendor/Third-Party Model Ongoing Monitoring Specifics**
**SR 11-7 (Section VII):** *"Sound practice involves conducting ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis to assess whether vendor models are accurate, remain fit for purpose, and continue to be reliable... appropriately documenting, justifying, and evaluating adjustments made to customize the model."*

**SOP Gap:** While third-party models are **in scope** (Section 1.2 table), the procedures **do not address**:
- How to perform outcomes analysis when vendor model internals (code, training data, methodology) are proprietary.
- Contractual SLAs for vendor-provided monitoring data / ground truth.
- Documentation of any **customizations/overlays** applied to vendor models (required by SR 11-7).
- Independent validation of vendor model performance claims post-deployment.

---

### 5. **Effective Challenge / Independent Monitoring Review**
**SR 11-7 (Section III):** *"Sound model risk management also involves 'effective challenge,' which refers to the critical analysis conducted by objective experts who evaluate model risk and effect appropriate changes throughout the model lifecycle... sufficient independence to maintain objectivity."*

**SOP Gap:** Monitoring is performed by **MLOps and Model Owners** (the same teams that build/deploy). The SOP **does not require**:
- Periodic independent review of monitoring effectiveness by a separate validation/audit function.
- "Effective challenge" of monitoring thresholds, drift metrics, or alert fatigue by objective experts.
- Internal Audit evaluation of whether the monitoring program itself is rigorous (SR 11-7: *"internal audit's role is generally to evaluate whether the model risk management practices are rigorous and effective"*).

---

### 6. **Model Inventory Content Requirements**
**SR 11-7 (Section VI):** *"An effective model inventory includes sufficient information to understand model risks, so as to support effective model risk management at the individual and aggregate levels."*

**SOP Gap:** The SOP references the **MLflow Model Registry** (Section 5.1) but **does not specify** the minimum inventory fields required by SR 11-7, such as:
- Model purpose, scope, and **limitations**.
- Materiality/risk tier.
- Data lineage and key assumptions.
- Validation status and date.
- Vendor vs. internal designation.
- Interdependencies with other models.

---

### 7. **Documentation for Continuity, Recommendations & Exceptions Tracking**
**SR 11-7 (Section VI):** *"Adequate documentation helps to support effective model risk management... tracking of recommendations, responses, and exceptions; it can also be used to more effectively help manage any model remediation efforts."*

**SOP Gap:** The SOP has incident logs, post-mortems, and ServiceNow exception requests, but **lacks a centralized, searchable system** to:
- Track **all** monitoring-related recommendations (from validation, audit, RCA) to closure.
- Link exceptions to specific models and monitor their expiration.
- Ensure continuity of operations if key personnel depart (e.g., documented runbooks beyond the playbook).

---

### 8. **Monitoring Frequency & Scope Tied to Materiality (Not Just Model Type)**
**SR 11-7 (Section V):** *"The frequency and scope of monitoring reports will depend on the nature of the model, the availability of new data or modeling approaches, and model materiality."*

**SOP Gap:** The SOP uses **fixed windows** (1hr, 24hr, 7 days) and **uniform thresholds** by model type (Clinical/Financial/Operational). It **does not**:
- Define materiality tiers (e.g., Tier 1 = high financial/clinical impact) with differentiated monitoring intensity.
- Adjust monitoring scope based on data availability (e.g., models with 90-day ground-truth latency get less real-time performance monitoring—acknowledged in 5.2.2 but not tied to a risk-based framework).

---

### 9. **Pre-Deployment Monitoring Response Procedures**
**SR 11-7 (Section V):** *"An effective ongoing monitoring plan may also include... procedures for responding to any issues that may occur, before and after a model is approved for use."*

**SOP Gap:** The SOP’s **Degradation Response Playbook (Section 5.5)** and **Exception Handling (Section 8)** are **post-deployment only**. No procedures exist for:
- Responding to monitoring signals during **shadow mode / A/B testing** (pre-approval).
- Criteria to **block promotion** based on monitoring results during the 60-minute bake (Section 6.1 mentions automated halt but not a formal response procedure).

---

### 10. **User Feedback Integration into Monitoring**
**SR 11-7 (Section IV):** *"User feedback provides business insights that enhance future development. Constructive engagement, particularly around model design, assumptions, and outcomes, strengthens both model understanding and model quality."*

**SOP Gap:** The SOP **does not collect or incorporate** end-user (clinician, underwriter, operator) feedback as a monitoring input. No mechanism to:
- Capture override rates, user complaints, or "model disagreement" signals.
- Feed qualitative feedback into drift/performance investigations.

---

### 11. **Explicit Model Adjustment / Recalibration / Redevelopment Triggers**
**SR 11-7 (Section V):** *"When performance deviates meaningfully from expectations, banking organizations generally consider whether model adjustments, recalibration, or redevelopment are warranted."*

**SOP Gap:** The SOP’s playbook focuses on **immediate mitigation** (rollback, fallback, feature-off). The **7-day escalation (Section 8.2)** triggers a "Remediation or Sunset Review" but **does not define**:
- Quantitative thresholds that distinguish "recalibrate" vs. "redevelop" vs. "sunset."
- A structured recalibration workflow (data refresh, retraining, re-validation) as a standard response.

---

## Summary Table

| SR 11-7 Expectation | SOP-AIML-006 Status |
|---------------------|----------------------|
| Outcomes analysis (back-testing, outlier analysis) | ❌ Missing |
| Periodic model limitations reassessment | ❌ Missing |
| Aggregate/portfolio risk monitoring | ❌ Missing |
| Vendor model monitoring specifics | ⚠️ Partial (in scope, no tailored procedures) |
| Effective challenge / independent review | ❌ Missing |
| Model inventory content requirements | ⚠️ Partial (registry exists, content not specified) |
| Documentation for continuity & exception tracking | ⚠️ Partial (incidents/exceptions tracked, not centralized) |
| Materiality-based monitoring frequency/scope | ❌ Missing (fixed by model type) |
| Pre-approval monitoring response procedures | ❌ Missing |
| User feedback integration | ❌ Missing |
| Explicit recalibration/redevelopment triggers | ⚠️ Partial (escalation exists, criteria undefined) |

---

**Compliance level: gap**

Model validation evaluates whether models perform as expected and includes an 
assessment of a model’s reliability and its limitations. The nature and rigor of validation generally

limitations and errors and clarifies appropriate use and whether corrective actions may be

characterize the source and extent of the model risk. Validation can reveal performance 
deterioration over time and inform judgments about acceptable performance ranges. When 
performance deviates meaningfully from expectations, banking organizations generally consider 
whether model adjustments, recalibration, or redevelopment are warranted.  
The timing, nature, and frequency of validation activities vary based on model purpose, 
model methodology, frequency and scope of model changes, data limitations, and other practical 
constraints. Sound practice recognizes that validation approaches may differ across models based

All components of the model lifecycle benefit from model governance that is supported

and establish a framework for assessing the magnitude of model risk and for applying model risk

Aggregate risk reflects interactions and dependencies among models; reliance on common

Based on my review of SOP-CLIN-005 against the NIST AI RMF MEASURE function (NIST AI 100-1) and the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1), here are the **specific missing elements** organized by MEASURE subcategory.

---

## MEASURE 1: Appropriate methods and metrics are identified and applied

### MEASURE 1.1 — Risk-based metric selection & documentation of unmeasured risks
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **No explicit linkage to a MAP function risk enumeration** — The SOP defines performance thresholds (ECE < 0.05, sensitivity CI > 0.85) but does not show how these metrics were selected based on prioritized risks identified in a MAP-phase risk assessment. | MS-1.1-001: “Identify and document approaches and metrics for measuring GAI risks enumerated during the MAP function… starting with the most significant AI risks.” | Section 5.1 sets thresholds but does not reference a prior risk mapping or justify why *these* metrics address the *most significant* risks. |
| **No process to track and document risks that cannot be measured quantitatively** (e.g., long-term societal trust, emergent behavioral risks). | MS-1.1-009: “Track and document risks or opportunities related to all GAI risks that cannot be measured quantitatively, including explanations as to why some risks cannot be measured.” | Entirely absent. The SOP assumes all relevant risks are captured by AUC, ECE, subgroup deltas. |
| **No structured human-feedback / red-teaming exercises defined for risk measurement** (beyond the one-time Human Factors evaluation in §5.5). | MS-1.1-008: “Define use cases, contexts of use, capabilities, and negative impacts where structured human feedback exercises, e.g., GAI red-teaming, would be most beneficial.” | §5.5 is a pre-release simulation; no ongoing red-teaming or structured feedback from affected communities (patients, clinicians) is mandated. |
| **No continuous monitoring of equity impacts via direct community feedback** — only statistical subgroup monitoring. | MS-1.1-006: “Implement continuous monitoring of GAI system impacts to identify whether GAI outputs are equitable across various sub-populations. Seek active and direct feedback from affected communities via structured feedback mechanisms or red-teaming.” | §7.2 does monthly statistical trending; no mechanism for *direct patient/community feedback* on perceived fairness or harm. |

### MEASURE 1.2 — Regular reassessment of metric appropriateness & control effectiveness
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **No defined process to periodically review whether the chosen metrics (AUC, ECE, sensitivity, etc.) remain appropriate** as clinical practice, patient populations, or model capabilities evolve. | MS-1.2-001: “Regularly assess the appropriateness of metrics and effectiveness of controls for measuring GAI risks… update based on new research, incidents, or stakeholder feedback.” | §7.3 (QBR) reviews *performance trends* but not *metric validity* or *control effectiveness*. |
| **No explicit incorporation of error reports or near-miss analyses into metric/control updates.** | MS-1.2-002: “Incorporate reports of errors, near misses, and potential impacts on affected communities into the assessment of metric appropriateness.” | §10 (Exceptions) handles deviations; no systematic error/near-miss feed into metric review. |

### MEASURE 1.3 — Independent assessment & external stakeholder consultation
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **No requirement that independent assessors be external to the organization** — the Clinical Validation Lead is internal (albeit separate from development). | MS-1.3-001/002: “Engage in internal and external evaluations… in consultation with representative AI Actors with expertise… and/or who are representative of the populations associated with the context of use.” | Medical Advisory Board is external but its role is advisory (§3), not a mandated independent assessment with structured feedback exercises. |
| **No verification that evaluators are not involved in system development** (beyond the RACI separation). | MS-1.3-003: “Verify those conducting structured human feedback exercises are not directly involved in system development tasks for the same GAI model.” | RACI separates roles but no formal attestation or conflict-of-interest check for *evaluation* activities (e.g., Human Factors, red-teaming). |

---

## MEASURE 2: AI systems are evaluated for trustworthy characteristics

### MEASURE 2.1 — TEVV documentation (test sets, metrics, tools)
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **No documentation of the *tools* used for TEVV** (e.g., MLflow/LangSmith versions, custom scripts, statistical libraries). | MS-2.1-001: “Document test sets, metrics, and details about the tools used during TEVV.” | §5.3 mentions “Meridian Clinical ML Observability Platform (customized MLflow and LangSmith stack)” but no versioning, configuration, or tool qualification records are required. |

### MEASURE 2.2 — Human-subject evaluation protections & representativeness
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **No explicit IRB / human-subject protection requirements** for the Human Factors evaluation (§5.5) or the Independent Clinical Validation (§5.4) when they involve clinician interaction with live patient data. | MS-2.2-001: “Ensure evaluations involving human subjects meet applicable requirements (including human subject protection) and are representative of the relevant population.” | §5.4 references “blind-chart-review” and §5.5 “simulated clinical environment” but no IRB, informed consent, or representativeness criteria are mandated. |

### MEASURE 2.3 — Performance/assurance criteria measured in deployment-like conditions
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **Silent Mode (§5.7) is only 14 days and limited to technical drift/latency** — no requirement to measure clinical performance criteria (sensitivity, calibration) under *real* deployment conditions before full release. | MS-2.3-001: “Measure AI system performance or assurance criteria… for conditions similar to deployment setting(s).” | Silent Mode explicitly *suppresses* clinical output; no “shadow-mode with clinical outcome capture” phase is required. |

### MEASURE 2.4 — Production monitoring of functionality & behavior
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **No monitoring of *model behavior* beyond drift, latency, and confidence rates** — e.g., no monitoring for emergent failure modes, adversarial inputs, or changes in explanation quality. | MS-2.4-001: “Monitor the functionality and behavior of the AI system and its components… when in production.” | §7.1 tracks only the four KPIs listed; no behavioral / functional monitoring (e.g., output distribution shifts, explanation fidelity). |

### MEASURE 2.5 — Validity, reliability, and generalizability limitations documented
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **Generalizability limitations are only addressed via subgroup analysis (§5.8)** — no systematic documentation of *out-of-distribution* failure modes, temporal degradation bounds, or geographic/site-specific limitations beyond the independent validation site. | MS-2.5-001: “Document limitations of generalizability beyond the conditions under which the technology was developed.” | §5.8 flags subgroup disparities; no dedicated “Generalizability Limitations” section in the release package. |

### MEASURE 2.6 / 2.7 — Security & resilience evaluation (GenAI Profile)
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **No AI red-teaming program** for prompt injection, adversarial examples, data poisoning, model extraction, or membership inference. | MS-2.7-007: “Perform AI red-teaming to assess resilience against: Abuse to facilitate attacks… GAI attacks (e.g., prompt injection), ML attacks (e.g., adversarial examples/prompts, data poisoning, membership inference, model extraction, sponge examples).” | TC-04 (Adversarial Input Filter) is a *runtime filter*, not a *pre-deployment red-teaming evaluation*. No periodic red-teaming mandated. |
| **No benchmarking of security/resilience against industry standards** (e.g., MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI 100-2). | MS-2.7-002: “Benchmark GAI system security and resilience related to content provenance against industry standards and best practices.” | Absent. |
| **No measurement of content provenance / authentication reliability** (relevant if the system generates clinical reports or summaries). | MS-2.7-005: “Measure reliability of content authentication methods, such as watermarking, cryptographic signatures… Evaluate the rate of false positives and false negatives in content provenance.” | Not addressed. Policy 4.5 requires “confidence scores in natural language” but no provenance/watermarking for generated text. |

### MEASURE 2.9 — Explainability, validation, and contextual interpretation
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **No systematic explanation generation or validation** (counterfactuals, gradient attributions, surrogate models, occlusion studies). | MS-2.9-001: “Apply and document ML explanation results such as: Analysis of embeddings, Counterfactual prompts, Gradient-based attributions, Model compression/surrogate models, Occlusion/term reduction.” | §4.5 and §5.5 address *presentation* of confidence scores; no requirement to *generate, validate, or document* model explanations. |
| **No documentation of model details for responsible use** (architecture, training objectives, RLHF/fine-tuning, data provenance, ethical considerations). | MS-2.9-002: “Document GAI model details including: Proposed use and organizational value; Assumptions and limitations, Data collection methodologies; Data provenance; Data quality; Model architecture… Optimization objectives; Training algorithms; RLHF approaches; Fine-tuning or RAG approaches; Evaluation data; Ethical considerations; Legal and regulatory requirements.” | The Clinical Performance Protocol (§5.1) covers some of this but not comprehensively (e.g., no training algorithm details, no ethical considerations section, no data provenance chain). |

### MEASURE 2.10 — Privacy risk examination
| Missing Element | NIST AI 600-1 Reference | SOP Gap |
|-----------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **No privacy-specific red-teaming or measurement** (training data extraction, membership inference, PII leakage, location tracking). | MS-2.10-001: “Conduct AI red-teaming to assess issues such as: Outputting of training data samples… membership inference risks; Revealing biometric, confidential, copyrighted, licensed, patented, personal, proprietary, sensitive, or trade-marked information.” | TC-01 (Input Integrity Guard) and HIPAA-compliant logs (§6.1) protect *inputs*; no evaluation of whether *model outputs* leak training data or enable re-identification. |

---

## Cross-cutting GenAI Profile Risks Not Addressed

| GenAI Risk (NIST AI 600-1 §2) | SOP Coverage | Gap |
|-------------------------------|--------------|-----|
| **2.2 Confabulation** (hallucination in generated reports) | Not addressed — SOP assumes discriminative models; if any generative component (e.g., report synthesis) exists, no confabulation detection/measurement is defined. | No metric, monitoring, or red-teaming for confabulation. |
| **2.7 Human-AI Configuration** (automation bias, over-reliance) | Partially addressed in §5.5 (Human Factors) but no *ongoing measurement* of automation bias in production. | MS-1.1-006, MS-2.7-003 call for user surveys / feedback on over-reliance; absent. |
| **2.8 Information Integrity** (synthetic content indistinguishable from real) | Not addressed — no content provenance, watermarking, or detection for AI-generated clinical notes. | MS-2.7-002, MS-2.7-005. |
| **2.12 Value Chain / Component Integration** (third-party model/library risks) | Not addressed — no measurement of risks from pre-trained backbones, open-source libraries, or vendor components. | GenAI Profile §2.12, Appendix A.1.3. |
| **2.5 Environmental Impacts** | Not measured. | MS-1.1-007 (data quality/provenance) could extend to compute/environmental tracking; absent. |

---

## Summary of Missing Elements by Priority

| Priority | Missing Element | MEASURE Subcategory |
|----------|-----------------|---------------------|
| **Critical** | No AI red-teaming program (adversarial, privacy, security) | 2.7, 2.10 |
| **Critical** | No documentation of unmeasured risks / residual risk register | 1.1 (MS-1.1-009) |
| **High** | No periodic reassessment of metric appropriateness & control effectiveness | 1.2 |
| **High** | No external independent assessment with structured community feedback | 1.3 |
| **High** | No human-subject protection (IRB) requirements for clinical validation / human factors | 2.2 |
| **High** | No systematic explainability generation, validation, or documentation | 2.9 |
| **Medium** | No deployment-like clinical performance measurement before full release (shadow mode with outcomes) | 2.3 |
| **Medium** | No production monitoring of model behavior / emergent failure modes | 2.4 |
| **Medium** | No generalizability limitations documentation beyond subgroup analysis | 2.5 |
| **Medium** | No TEVV tool versioning / configuration documentation | 2.1 |
| **Medium** | No third-party component risk measurement (value chain) | GenAI §2.12 |
| **Lower** | No environmental impact measurement | GenAI §2.5 |
| **Lower** | No content provenance / watermarking for generated outputs (if applicable) | 2.7 |

---

## Compliance level: gap

The SOP is strong on **statistical validation, calibration, subgroup fairness, and production monitoring** for discriminative diagnostic models. However, it has **significant gaps** relative to the NIST AI RMF MEASURE function — particularly in **risk-based metric selection (MEASURE 1), independent external assessment (MEASURE 1.3), security/resilience red-teaming (MEASURE 2.7), privacy risk measurement (MEASURE 2.10), explainability validation (MEASURE 2.9), and documentation of unmeasured risks**. These gaps are material for any system that incorporates generative components or operates in a high-stakes clinical environment where the GenAI Profile’s additional risks (confabulation, automation bias, information integrity, value-chain) are relevant.

5.3 Measure
The MEASURE function employs quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-method tools, tech-
niques, and methodologies to analyze, assess, benchmark, and monitor AI risk and related
impacts. It uses knowledge relevant to AI risks identified in the MAP function and informs
the MANAGE function. AI systems should be tested before their deployment and regu-
larly while in operation. AI risk measurements include documenting aspects of systems’
functionality and trustworthiness.
Measuring AI risks includes tracking metrics for trustworthy characteristics, social impact,
and human-AI configurations. Processes developed or adopted in the MEASURE function
should include rigorous software testing and performance assessment methodologies with
associated measures of uncertainty, comparisons to performance benchmarks, and formal-
ized reporting and documentation of results. Processes for independent review can improve
the effectiveness of testing and can mitigate internal biases and potential conflicts of inter-
est.
Where tradeoffs among the trustworthy characteristics arise, measurement provides a trace-
able basis to inform management decisions. Options may include recalibration, impact
mitigation, or removal of the system from design, development, production, or use, as well
as a range of compensating, detective, deterrent, directive, and recovery controls.
After completing the MEASURE function, objective, repeatable, or scalable test, evaluation,
verification, and validation (TEVV) processes including metrics, methods, and methodolo-
gies are in place, followed, and documented. Metrics and measurement methodologies
should adhere to scientific, legal, and ethical norms and be carried out in an open and trans-
parent process. New types of measurement, qualitative and quantitative, may need to be
developed. The degree to which each measurement type provides unique and meaningful
information to the assessment of AI risks should be considered. Framework users will en-
hance their capacity to comprehensively evaluate system trustworthiness, identify and track
existing and emergent risks, and verify efficacy of the metrics. Measurement outcomes will
be utilized in the MANAGE function to assist risk monitoring and response efforts. It is in-
cumbent on Framework users to continue applying the MEASURE function to AI systems
as knowledge, methodologies, risks, and impacts evolve over time.

1. Introduction 
This document is a cross-sectoral proﬁle of and companion resource for the AI Risk Management 
Framework (AI RMF 1.0) for Generative AI,1 pursuant to President Biden’s Executive Order (EO) 14110 on 
Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Artiﬁcial Intelligence.2 The AI RMF was released in January 2023, and is 
intended for voluntary use and to improve the ability of organizations to incorporate trustworthiness 
considerations into the design, development, use, and evaluation of AI products, services, and systems.  
A proﬁle is an implementation of the AI RMF functions, categories, and subcategories for a speciﬁc 
setting, application, or technology – in this case, Generative AI (GAI) – based on the requirements, risk 
tolerance, and resources of the Framework user. AI RMF proﬁles assist organizations in deciding how to 
best manage AI risks in a manner that is well-aligned with their goals, considers legal/regulatory 
requirements and best practices, and reﬂects risk management priorities. Consistent with other AI RMF 
proﬁles, this proﬁle oﬀers insights into how risk can be managed across various stages of the AI lifecycle 
and for GAI as a technology.  
As GAI covers risks of models or applications that can be used across use cases or sectors, this document 
is an AI RMF cross-sectoral proﬁle. Cross-sectoral proﬁles can be used to govern, map, measure, and 
manage risks associated with activities or business processes common across sectors, such as the use of 
large language models (LLMs), cloud-based services, or acquisition. 
This document deﬁnes risks that are novel to or exacerbated by the use of GAI. After introducing and 
describing these risks, the document provides a set of suggested actions to help organizations govern, 
map, measure, and manage these risks.

Value Chain and Component Integration GAI value chains involve many third-party components such as procured datasets, pre-trained models, and software libraries. These components might be improperly obtained or not properly vetted, leading to diminished transparency or accountability for downstream users. While this is a risk for traditional AI systems and some other digital technologies, the risk is exacerbated for GAI due to the scale of the training data, which may be too large for humans to vet; the diﬃculty of training foundation models, which leads to extensive reuse of limited numbers of models; and the extent to which GAI may be integrated into other devices and services. As GAI systems often involve many distinct third-party components and data sources, it may be diﬃcult to attribute issues in a system’s behavior to any one of these sources. Errors in third-party GAI components can also have downstream impacts on accuracy and robustness. For example, test datasets commonly used to benchmark or validate models can contain label errors. Inaccuracies in these labels can impact the “stability” or robustness of these benchmarks, which many GAI practitioners consider during the model selection process. Trustworthy AI Characteristics: Accountable and Transparent, Explainable and Interpretable, Fair with Harmful Bias Managed, Privacy Enhanced, Safe, Secure and Resilient, Valid and Reliable 3. Other practical approaches for AI safety often relate to rigorous simulation and in-domain testing, real-time monitoring, and the ability to shut down, modify, or have human inter- vention into systems that deviate from intended or expected functionality. AI safety risk management approaches should take cues from efforts and guidelines for safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or application-specific guidelines or standards. 3.3 Secure and Resilient AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be re- silient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their envi- ronment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted from: ISO /IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples, data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Manage- ment Framework are among those which are applicable here. Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the abil- ity to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes re- silience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data. 3.4 Accountable and Transparent Trustworthy AI depends upon accountability. Accountability presupposes transparency. Transparencyreflects the extent to which information about an AI system and its outputs is available to individuals interacting with such a system – regardless of whether they are even aware that they are doing so. Meaningful transparency provides access to appropriate levels of information based on the stage of the AI lifecycle and tailored to the role or knowledge of AI actors or individuals interacting with or using the AI system. By promoting higher levels of understanding, transparency increases confidence in the AI system. 10 GAI systems can ease the unintentional production or dissemination of false, inaccurate, or misleading content (misinformation) at scale, particularly if the content stems from confabulations. GAI systems can also ease the deliberate production or dissemination of false or misleading information (disinformation) at scale, where an actor has the explicit intent to deceive or cause harm to others. Even very subtle changes to text or images can manipulate human and machine perception. Similarly, GAI systems could enable a higher degree of sophistication for malicious actors to produce disinformation that is targeted towards speciﬁc demographics. Current and emerging multimodal models make it possible to generate both text-based disinformation and highly realistic “deepfakes” – that is, synthetic audiovisual content and photorealistic images.12 Additional disinformation threats could be enabled by future GAI models trained on new data modalities. Disinformation and misinformation – both of which may be facilitated by GAI – may erode public trust in true or valid evidence and information, with downstream eﬀects. For example, a synthetic image of a Pentagon blast went viral and brieﬂy caused a drop in the stock market. Generative AI models can also assist malicious actors in creating compelling imagery and propaganda to support disinformation campaigns, which may not be photorealistic, but could enable these campaigns to gain more reach and engagement on social media platforms. question.question: Reviewing SOP-AIML-009 (Algorithmic Bias Detection and Mitigation) against GDPR Article 35 (DPIA) and Article 22 (automated decision-making), what specific procedures are MISSING?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) procedure under Article 35 — systematic description of processing, necessity/proportionality assessment, risks-to-rights evaluation, measures envisaged; (2) prior-consultation procedure with the supervisory authority (Article 36) when residual risk remains high; (3) Article 22 procedures for solely-automated significant-effect decisions — meaningful information about the logic involved, right to obtain human intervention, right to express the data subject's point of view, right to contest the decision; (4) Articles 13/14 specificity in privacy notices regarding the bias-detection processing and its purposes.
question.notes: Gap detection across multiple GDPR articles for a bias SOP.

Based on my review of SOP-AIML-009 against GDPR Article 35 (DPIA) and Article 22 (automated decision-making), here are the **specific missing procedures**:

---

### **I. Article 35 DPIA Gaps**

| # | GDPR Requirement | SOP Status | Missing Procedure |
|---|------------------|------------|-------------------|
| **1** | **Mandatory DPIA trigger for automated decision-making** (Art. 35(3)(a)): "systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects…based on automated processing, including profiling, and on which decisions are based that produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect the natural person" | SOP references SOP-PRI-008 for DPIAs but **does not mandate a DPIA for every in-scope AI/ML system** (clinical risk scoring, credit scoring, adverse event prediction all meet this trigger). | **Add a mandatory DPIA initiation step in Phase 1 (Pre-Development)** that automatically triggers a DPIA for all Critical/High-risk models per the Model Risk Tier, with a documented determination recorded in the Bias Testing Plan. |
| **2** | **Systematic description of processing operations** (Art. 35(7)(a)): purposes, nature, scope, context | Bias Testing Plan captures decision context and fairness metrics but **not a full processing description** (data flows, retention, recipients, legal basis, profiling logic). | **Extend the Bias Testing Plan template** to include: (a) categories of personal/special-category data; (b) profiling logic summary; (c) legal basis per Art. 6/9; (d) data flows and third-country transfers; (e) retention periods. |
| **3** | **Necessity and proportionality assessment** (Art. 35(7)(b)) | **Absent.** No step evaluates whether automated processing is necessary vs. less intrusive alternatives, or whether scope is proportionate. | **Insert a Necessity & Proportionality Assessment** in Phase 1, signed by Product Manager and EU DPO, documenting: why automated processing is required, why non-automated alternatives are insufficient, and why data scope is proportionate. |
| **4** | **Risk assessment to rights and freedoms** (Art. 35(7)(c)) | Fairness metrics assess bias risk but **not broader GDPR risks** (e.g., loss of control over data, discrimination beyond protected attributes, chilling effects, function creep). | **Add a GDPR Risk Assessment matrix** alongside fairness assessment, covering: discrimination, loss of autonomy, opacity, data security, function creep, and special-category data risks. |
| **5** | **Measures to address risks** (Art. 35(7)(d)): safeguards, security, compliance demonstration | Mitigation hierarchy (Sec. 5.5) addresses bias only. **Missing**: pseudonymisation, encryption, access controls, data subject rights enablement, contractual safeguards for vendors. | **Expand the BiasComplianceCheck (Sec. 5.4)** to verify Art. 35(7)(d) measures: pseudonymisation in training, encryption at rest/in transit, vendor DPAs, data subject rights tooling. |
| **6** | **Seek views of data subjects or representatives** (Art. 35(9)) | **Completely absent.** No mechanism for patient/customer consultation on automated decision-making. | **Add a Data Subject Consultation step** in Phase 1 for Critical/High-risk models: publish a plain-language summary of the automated decision logic, purposes, and safeguards; collect feedback via a defined channel; document outcomes in the DPIA. |
| **7** | **DPIA review upon change of risk** (Art. 35(11)) | Monitoring (Sec. 5.6) tracks bias drift but **does not trigger DPIA re-assessment** when model purpose, data sources, or deployment context change. | **Add a DPIA Review Trigger** in Sec. 5.6: any change to model purpose, new data categories, new deployment geography, or significant logic change → mandatory DPIA review with EU DPO sign-off. |
| **8** | **Prior consultation with supervisory authority** (Art. 36) where residual high risk remains | **Not addressed.** No procedure for consulting the relevant DPA when DPIA indicates unmitigated high risk. | **Add an Escalation Path** in Sec. 8.3: if DPIA review (Sec. 35(11)) or IRB identifies residual high risk that cannot be mitigated → Legal/Compliance initiates Art. 36 consultation with the lead supervisory authority. |

---

### **II. Article 22 Automated Decision-Making Gaps**

| # | GDPR Requirement | SOP Status | Missing Procedure |
|---|------------------|------------|-------------------|
| **9** | **Document lawful basis for solely automated decisions** (Art. 22(2)): contract necessity, Union/Member State law, or explicit consent | SOP assumes human-in-the-loop (Sec. 4.3) but **does not document which Art. 22(2) exception applies** for each model, nor verify that the exception’s conditions are met. | **Add a Lawful Basis Determination** in Phase 1 for every model: record which Art. 22(2) exception applies (a/b/c), attach evidence (contract terms, statutory citation, consent records), and have Legal sign off. |
| **10** | **Safeguards when exceptions apply** (Art. 22(3)): right to human intervention, to express point of view, to contest the decision | Sec. 4.3 mandates human *reviewer* oversight but **does not grant data subjects** the right to request human intervention, express their view, or contest the outcome. | **Implement a Data Subject Contest Procedure**: (a) automated decision notice to data subject with outcome and logic summary; (b) dedicated channel (portal/email/phone) to request human review; (c) SLA for human reconsideration (e.g., 15 business days); (d) documentation of contest outcome. |
| **11** | **Meaningful information about logic, significance, consequences** (Art. 22(3), Art. 15(1)(h)) | Model Cards (Sec. 4.5, 5.4) are **internal documents**; no procedure to provide data subjects with accessible explanations of the logic, significance, and envisaged consequences. | **Create a Data Subject Explanation Layer**: for each production model, generate a plain-language "Algorithmic Decision Notice" covering: (a) what the model predicts; (b) key factors/logic (non-technical); (c) significance for the individual; (d) how to contest. Publish at decision time (e.g., in patient portal, loan decision letter). |
| **12** | **Right to object to profiling** (Art. 21) linked to automated decisions | **No objection mechanism** for profiling that feeds automated decisions. | **Add an Objection Handling Workflow**: data subject objection → suppress automated processing for that individual → route to manual review → document outcome. Integrate with existing DSAR process (SOP-PRI-008). |
| **13** | **Special-category data conditions** (Art. 9(2)) for health/financial profiling | Clinical and HealthPay models process special-category data (health, genetic, biometric). SOP mentions PHI/PII but **does not verify Art. 9(2) condition** (explicit consent, substantial public interest, etc.) for each model. | **Add an Art. 9(2) Condition Check** in Phase 1 Privacy Consultation: for each special-category data element, record the applicable Art. 9(2) ground and attach supporting evidence (consent records, legal opinion, etc.). |

---

### **III. Cross-Cutting Governance Gaps**

| # | Gap | Required Action |
|---|-----|-----------------|
| **14** | **No DPIA register / Art. 30 ROPA linkage** | Maintain a DPIA register linked to the Record of Processing Activities (Art. 30), with model ID, DPIA date, review date, and residual risk rating. |
| **15** | **No automated decision-making inventory** (Art. 30(1)(g) + EDPB guidance) | Create and maintain an inventory of all solely/partially automated decisions producing legal/similarly significant effects, with lawful basis, safeguards, and DPIA reference. |
| **16** | **Vendor/third-party model DPIA coverage** (Art. 28, Art. 35) | Sec. A-03 requires vendor fairness attestation but **not vendor DPIA review** or Art. 28 DPA verification for procured models/APIs. |

---

### **Summary of Required SOP Amendments**

1. **Phase 1 (Pre-Development)**: Add mandatory DPIA initiation, Necessity/Proportionality Assessment, Lawful Basis Determination (Art. 22/9), Data Subject Consultation plan, and Art. 9(2) Condition Check.
2. **Phase 4 (Pre-Deployment)**: Expand BiasComplianceCheck to verify Art. 35(7)(d) measures, Art. 22(3) safeguards (contest procedure, explanation layer), and DPIA sign-off by EU DPO.
3. **Phase 6 (Monitoring)**: Add DPIA review triggers (Art. 35(11)) and Art. 36 escalation path.
4. **New Appendix**: Data Subject Contest Procedure, Algorithmic Decision Notice template, Automated Decision Inventory.

---

**Compliance level: gap** — The SOP addresses algorithmic bias thoroughly but lacks the GDPR-mandated DPIA framework, Article 22 safeguards for data subjects (contest, explanation, objection), lawful basis documentation, and special-category data condition verification for automated decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects.

### Article 4 — Definitions

For the purposes of this Regulation:

‘profiling’ means any form of automated processing of personal data consisting of the use of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person, in particular to analyse or predict aspects concerning that natural person’s performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behaviour, location or movements;

‘pseudonymisation’ means the processing of personal data in such a manner that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures to ensure that the personal data are not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person;

question.question: Reviewing SOP-PENG-001 (Secure Software Development Lifecycle) against EU AI Act Article 9 (risk management system), what specific elements are MISSING for an SDLC supporting high-risk AI systems?
question.expected_answer: Missing: (1) continuous lifecycle risk-management process (Article 9 §2) — identification/analysis/estimation/evaluation of risks throughout development and after deployment, integrated into the SDLC phases; (2) elimination or reduction of identified risks through design and development decisions (Article 9 §4); (3) testing procedures explicitly verifying high-risk AI requirements against acceptable residual risk thresholds (Article 9 §6, §7); (4) consideration of foreseeable misuse and the use environment in risk assessment (Article 9 §3); (5) linkage to post-market-monitoring data feeding back into the SDLC (Article 9 §2 lifecycle loop).
question.notes: Gap detection — SDLC needs Article 9 lifecycle risk management baked in.

output.answer:
Based on my review of SOP-PENG-001 and EU AI Act Article 9, here are the **specific elements MISSING** for an SDLC supporting high-risk AI systems:

---

### 1. AI-Specific Risk Identification (Art. 9(2)(a))
**Missing:** The SOP's threat modeling (Section 5.2.2) uses **STRIDE**—a security-focused methodology covering Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, DoS, Elevation of Privilege. Article 9 requires identification of risks to **health, safety, and fundamental rights** (e.g., bias/discrimination, inaccurate clinical decisions, loss of autonomy, opacity). The SOP has no structured process for AI-specific hazard identification (model drift, data quality, representativeness, adversarial robustness, interpretability failures).

### 2. Reasonably Foreseeable Misuse Analysis (Art. 9(2)(b))
**Missing:** Article 9 explicitly requires risk estimation under **"conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse."** The SOP's "Abuser Stories" (Section 5.2.2) capture security misuse (e.g., brute-force login) but not AI misuse scenarios (e.g., off-label clinical use, input manipulation to trigger wrong predictions, deployment in populations not represented in training data).

### 3. Post-Market Monitoring Feedback Loop (Art. 9(2)(c) + Art. 72)
**Missing:** The SOP's Phase 6 (Operations) monitors CVEs and misconfigurations (Section 5.6) but **does not feed operational AI performance data (accuracy drift, fairness metrics, incident reports from deployers) back into the risk management system** as Article 9(2)(c) and Article 72 require. No defined process to re-evaluate risks from post-market data.

### 4. Integrated Risk Management Across All Section 2 Requirements (Art. 9(4))
**Missing:** Article 9(4) mandates that risk measures consider **"effects and possible interaction resulting from the combined application of the requirements set out in this Section"** (Articles 9–15: data governance, transparency, human oversight, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity). The SOP treats security, privacy, and quality as separate tracks; it has no mechanism to assess **cross-requirement interactions** (e.g., how a transparency measure affects security, or how human oversight impacts robustness).

### 5. Formal Residual Risk Acceptability Judgment (Art. 9(5))
**Missing:** The SOP records "residual risk" in the Threat Model Document (Section 5.2.2) but **lacks a documented, signed judgment that the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI system is "acceptable"** per Article 9(5). No defined acceptability criteria or approval authority for AI-specific residual risk.

### 6. Risk Elimination/Reduction Through AI Design Choices (Art. 9(5)(a))
**Missing:** The SOP's secure design checklist (Section 5.2.3) covers encryption, mTLS, secrets management—**not AI design decisions** that eliminate/reduce risk: model architecture selection, training data curation, fairness constraints, uncertainty quantification, fallback/rejection logic, or human-in-the-loop design points.

### 7. AI-Specific Mitigation Measures for Non-Eliminable Risks (Art. 9(5)(b))
**Missing:** No catalog of **AI-specific mitigations** for risks that cannot be designed out (e.g., runtime monitoring for distribution shift, confidence thresholds with deferral to human, adversarial input detection, model cards with known limitations).

### 8. Article 13 Transparency Information & Deployer Training (Art. 9(5)(c))
**Missing:** Article 9(5)(c) requires risk measures to include **"provision of information required pursuant to Article 13 and, where appropriate, training to deployers."** The SOP has no process to generate **Article 13-compliant instructions for use** (intended purpose, performance metrics, limitations, human oversight measures) or to deliver **deployer training**.

### 9. Continuous Iterative Risk Management Throughout Entire Lifecycle (Art. 9(2))
**Gap:** The SOP's risk activities are **phase-gated** (threat modeling at Design, scanning at Development/Testing, vuln management at Operations). Article 9 requires a **continuous iterative process** with "regular systematic review and updating" of the AI risk management system itself—not just vulnerability patching. No defined cadence or trigger for full AI risk management system review.

### 10. Documented AI Risk Management System (Art. 9(1))
**Missing:** Article 9(1) requires a risk management system that is **"established, implemented, documented and maintained."** The SOP documents an SSDLC; it does not document a **standalone AI risk management system** with its own scope, roles, methods, records, and review cycle specific to high-risk AI.

### 11. Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Art. 27)
**Missing:** For high-risk AI systems, **Article 27 requires a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA)** before deployment. The SOP references no FRIA process, template, or responsible role.

### 12. AI-Specific Data Governance Integration (Art. 10)
**Missing:** Article 10 (data governance) requires training/validation/testing data sets to be "relevant, sufficiently representative, free of errors and complete." The SOP's data classification (Section 1.2, Section 4.2) addresses PHI/PII but **not representativeness, bias assessment, or data quality metrics for AI training data**.

### 13. Human Oversight Design Requirements (Art. 14)
**Missing:** Article 14 mandates that high-risk AI systems be designed for **effective human oversight** (understanding, interpreting, deciding when to override). The SOP's design checklist (Section 5.2.3) has no human-oversight verification items.

### 14. Accuracy, Robustness, Cybersecurity Metrics (Art. 15)
**Missing:** Article 15 requires **declared and monitored levels of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity**. The SOP's KPIs (Section 7.2) track SAST findings, CVE MTTR, threat model coverage—**not model accuracy, robustness to distribution shift, or AI-specific cybersecurity metrics** (e.g., adversarial robustness, model extraction resistance).

---

### Summary Table

| Article 9 Requirement | SOP Coverage | Gap Severity |
|----------------------|--------------|--------------|
| 9(2)(a) AI risk ID (health/safety/fundamental rights) | STRIDE only (security) | **Critical** |
| 9(2)(b) Foreseeable misuse analysis | Security abuser stories only | **Critical** |
| 9(2)(c) Post-market monitoring feedback | CVE monitoring only | **Critical** |
| 9(4) Cross-requirement interaction analysis | None | **Critical** |
| 9(5) Residual risk acceptability judgment | Informal in TMD | **Critical** |
| 9(5)(a) Risk elimination via AI design | Secure design only | **Critical** |
| 9(5)(b) AI-specific mitigations | None | **Critical** |
| 9(5)(c) Art. 13 info + deployer training | None | **Critical** |
| 9(1)–9(2) Documented, iterative AI RMS | SSDLC ≠ AI RMS | **Critical** |
| Art. 27 FRIA | None | **Critical** |
| Art. 10 Data governance for AI | PHI classification only | **High** |
| Art. 14 Human oversight design | None | **High** |
| Art. 15 Accuracy/robustness metrics | None | **High** |

---

### Minimum Additions Needed for Article 9 Compliance

1. **New Section: "AI Risk Management System (per EU AI Act Art. 9)"** — standalone, cross-referenced from SSDLC phases.
2. **AI Hazard Taxonomy** — supplement STRIDE with AI-specific hazards (bias, inaccuracy, opacity, misuse, drift).
3. **Misuse Case Workshop** — mandatory for High-Impact AI features, distinct from security threat modeling.
4. **Post-Market Monitoring Plan (Art. 72)** — defined metrics, reporting channels, and feedback into risk management.
5. **Residual Risk Acceptance Record** — signed by CISO + Clinical Safety Officer + Compliance Officer.
6. **Article 13 Instructions-for-Use Generation** — integrated into Release phase (Phase 5).
7. **Deployer Training Package** — delivered with each high-risk AI release.
8. **FRIA Template & Process** — triggered at Requirements phase for high-risk AI.
9. **AI Data Governance Checklist** — representativeness, bias testing, provenance (Art. 10).
10. **Human Oversight Design Verification** — added to Design Review Checklist (Section 5.2.3).
11. **Art. 15 Metrics Dashboard** — accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity KPIs in Phase 6.

---

Compliance level: gap
